subject: physics
title: Luminosity, magnitude and astronomical distances
key_idea: A star's luminosity is its total power output. The intensity we receive falls with the square of the distance. Knowing a star's luminosity, or measuring its parallax, lets us find how far away it is.

sections.heading: Luminosity and the inverse square law

blocks.text: Two numbers describe how bright a star is. One is how much it gives out. The other is how much reaches us.

items.meaning: The total power of electromagnetic radiation emitted by a star, in watts.
The power received per unit area, measured at right angles to the radiation. It is also called radiant flux intensity, and is sometimes written F.

blocks.text: A star radiates equally in all directions. By the time the radiation is a distance d away, it is spread over a sphere of area 4πd².

items: Intensity is proportional to 1 ÷ d², so doubling the distance gives one quarter of the intensity.
The law assumes the star radiates equally in all directions.
It also assumes no radiation is absorbed or scattered on the way, which is not quite true in dusty space.

diagram.alt: A slider showing how luminosity and distance change the intensity received from a star.

items: Luminosity is the total power a star radiates. Intensity is the power arriving per square metre.
I = L ÷ (4πd²), so intensity falls with the square of the distance.
The law assumes equal radiation in all directions and no absorption.

blocks.text: Astronomical distances are huge, so metres are not convenient. Astronomers use three larger units.

rows: The mean distance from the Earth to the Sun
The distance light travels in a vacuum in one year
The distance at which 1 AU subtends an angle of 1 second of arc

blocks.text: Trigonometric parallax measures the distance to nearby stars. A nearby star seems to shift against the distant background stars as the Earth moves round its orbit.

items.text: Measure the position of the star against distant stars. Do it again six months later, when the Earth is on the opposite side of its orbit.
Find the angle the star appears to move through, and halve it.
This half-angle is the parallax, p. It is the angle at the star between the lines to the Earth and to the Sun.
Use the small angle and the Earth–Sun distance of 1 AU to find the distance.

blocks.label: Parallax and distance
where: p = parallax (seconds of arc, also called arcseconds)

items: One second of arc is 1/3600 of a degree.
A star with a parallax of 0.25 seconds of arc is 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4 pc away.
The nearer the star, the larger its parallax.
Parallax angles become too small to measure for stars that are far away, so the method works only for nearby stars.
1 pc is the distance at which 1 AU subtends 1 second of arc. 1 pc = 3.26 ly.
Parallax is half the apparent shift of a star over six months.
p = 1 ÷ d, with p in seconds of arc and d in parsec.

blocks.text: Parallax fails for distant stars and galaxies. Another way uses objects whose luminosity we already know.

items.text: Identify the object as a standard candle, such as a type Ia supernova or a Cepheid variable star, so its luminosity L is known.
Measure the intensity I received from it at the Earth.
Find d. This gives the distance to the galaxy that contains the standard candle.

items: Standard candles are bright enough to be seen in other galaxies, so they reach much further than parallax.
The dimmer a standard candle looks, the further away it is.
Dust between us and the object absorbs light, which makes the object seem further away than it is.
A standard candle has a known luminosity.
Comparing the known L with the measured I gives the distance, using I = L ÷ (4πd²).
Standard candles measure distances to galaxies, far beyond the reach of parallax.

checks.q: A star has a luminosity of 2.0 × 10²⁸ W. Calculate the intensity at the Earth, which is 3.0 × 10¹⁷ m away.
A star has a parallax of 0.050 seconds of arc. Calculate its distance in parsec and in light-years.
Explain how a standard candle is used to find the distance to a galaxy.
checks.a: A standard candle has a known luminosity. Measure the intensity received at the Earth. Use I = L ÷ (4πd²) and rearrange to find d. The standard candle's distance is the distance to its galaxy.

extra.heading: Detail this course asks for: apparent and absolute magnitude

blocks.text: Magnitude is an older way to rank how bright stars look. It is a subjective scale, based on what the eye sees, and the numbers run backwards.

items.meaning: How bright a star looks from the Earth, on the Hipparcos scale.
The apparent magnitude a star would have if it were at a distance of 10 pc.

items: The dimmest stars visible to the naked eye have a magnitude of 6.
A smaller magnitude means a brighter star.
A difference of 1 on the magnitude scale is an intensity ratio of 2.51.
Brightness is a subjective measure, as it depends on the observer. Intensity is an objective measure.
Absolute magnitude lets stars be compared fairly, as they are all placed at the same distance.

diagram.alt: A practice calculation of a star's distance in parsec from its apparent and absolute magnitudes.
diagram.question: A star has an apparent magnitude of {m} and an absolute magnitude of {M}. Calculate its distance in parsec.

items: A smaller apparent magnitude means a brighter star. The dimmest naked-eye stars are magnitude 6.
A magnitude difference of 1 is an intensity ratio of 2.51.
m – M = 5 log (d ÷ 10), with d in parsec.
